query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of aluminum (on the order of 2 atomic percent) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will enable the formation of an adherent, slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) surface scale during high‐temperature exposure, thereby greatly improving its oxygen resistance without sacrificing its beneficial mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification via the addition of ~2 at.% Al (introduced by substituting or adding to the base composition) to promote alumina scale formation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure at around 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) for durations on the order of 100 hours; mechanical testing at similar strain rates (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) as used for the baseline cast alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a coherent, continuous, and adherent Al2O3 passivation layer at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Due to aluminum’s high affinity for oxygen, even a minor addition preferentially forms a stable alumina (Al2O3) layer that impedes oxygen diffusion into the alloy. This passivation minimizes oxidation‐induced degradation while the bulk BCC microstructure and inherent solid solution strengthening remain largely intact, preserving the ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-modified alloy should exhibit significantly improved oxidation resistance (lower weight gain and thinner oxide scales) under high-temperature exposure while maintaining similar levels of tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strength at 1000 °C, with any changes being within ±10% of the baseline performance.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr showing poor oxygen resistance despite its useful mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: Intervention validity is assumed for oxygen exposures at ~1000 °C in air over 100-hour durations and under mechanical loading conditions similar to those reported for the base alloy; effects outside these conditions are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum aluminum content to balance oxidation protection with phase stability and mechanical properties is not precisely known and requires experimental optimization. The potential influence on secondary phase formations and any long‐term stability issues under cyclic oxidation are also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets: one of the baseline cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy and one modified with ~2 at.% Al. Subject both sets to identical thermal-oxidation treatment at 1000 °C in air for 100 hours. Following exposure, perform tensile tests at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (e.g., 1000 °C) under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹. Also, characterize the surface oxide scale (thickness, composition, and adherence) using microscopy and weight gain measurements.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and composition (via SEM/EDS, XRD)
Microstructural integrity of bulk phases (via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar oxide scale thickness and weight gain compared to the baseline) or if its ductility or yield strength deteriorates by more than ±10% relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that 2 at.% Al addition improves oxygen resistance without sacrificing mechanical performance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.
